name: The new sense of human power from machine production
plain_explanation: Industrial technology gave human beings, for the first time in history, the practical ability to reshape nature (moving mountains, creating waterfalls, making deserts bloom) and to reshape other people's minds (through mass education and propaganda) on a scale and speed never before possible, and Russell argues this new intoxication with power is one of the deepest forces reshaping modern philosophy and politics.
precise_definition: The claim that machine production -- alongside science and political revolt -- constitutes a third, largely non-philosophical source of nineteenth- and twentieth-century thought, whose chief effect is an unprecedented increase in the sense of human power, both over the non-human environment and, via scientific propaganda and education, of some human beings over others.
why_it_mattered: Russell presents framing a philosophy adequate to 'men intoxicated with the prospect of almost unlimited power' together with 'the apathy of the powerless' as 'the most pressing task of our time,' making this concept the chapter's forward-looking, almost programmatic conclusion.
historical_origin: Traced to the rise of industrialism from roughly the end of the eighteenth century onward.
associated_philosopher: Not attributed to one philosopher; Russell's own diagnostic category, illustrated via Carlyle's and the romantics' reaction to industrialism.
examples: An inconvenient mountain being 'abolished' and a convenient waterfall 'created'
Deserts made to blossom, or fertile regions turned to deserts, by human intervention
Authorities deciding what peasant children shall learn in school, transforming a population's mentality within a generation
influence_on_later_thinkers: Frames the tension, developed across the rest of Book Three, between an emphasis on 'the community as opposed to the individual' and traditional liberal individualism.
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Connected to the growing power of the State and to nationalism, and to the erosion of older fixed conceptions such as God and truth.
